## The question

This study asks whether the TDM could quantify the additional **Congested
Roadway Capacity Demand** — peak-period roadway burden — created by adding a
fixed number of typical households (500 or 1000) at different locations
around the region. Capturing that burden properly means letting the TDM run
its full multimodal, all-day pipeline for those households (mode choice,
trip timing, route choice) and measuring the *delay it imposes on everyone
else already on the system*, not just the new households' own travel.

The result would be expressed as a Burden Index relative to a reference
location at the region's geographic center (Murray): a household placed in
Western Davis County, for instance, might place meaningfully more burden on
the system than one placed in one of Davis County's designated City or Town
Centers.

## Decisions needed before building this

| Decision | Options | Recommendation | If left unresolved |
|---|---|---|---|
| **N** — households per site | 500 or 1000 | 1000, for a more clearly measurable effect | Defaults to 500 (the first-mentioned number in the original ask) |
| **Congestion threshold** | V/C ≥ 0.8, ≥ 1.0, or report both | Report both — cheap, since both are already in the same summary CSV | Defaults to reporting both |
| **Peak window** | AM+PM only, or all four periods | AM+PM, matching "peak-period" in the original ask; MD/EV available in the same file if wanted later | Defaults to AM+PM |
| **Site list** | See "Candidate sites" below — Murray control plus typical-vs-center pairs in Western Davis, SW Salt Lake, and western Utah counties (each with alternates) | Start with Murray + Syracuse pair (minimal proof-of-methodology build); once proven, expand to the full 7-site recommended list (Murray + 3 typical-vs-center pairs) | Build proceeds with the recommended picks below unless told otherwise |
| **Network vintage(s)** | 2023 (today) only, or 2023 + 2055 (long-range Needs) | Both — burden today, plus whether the center-vs-sprawl gap holds, widens, or narrows as the region grows to its 2055 forecast. More relevant to a growth-siting decision than a single-year snapshot | Proposed as part of the initial build, not a later add-on |

: {tbl-colwidths="[20,30,30,20]" .fixed-table}

## Proposed methodology

**Design:** one **Base** run, one **Control** run (Base + N
households added at a Murray TAZ — the geographic-center reference), and one
**Test** run per candidate site (Base + the same N households added at that
site's TAZ). Same household count everywhere, so differences reflect
*location*, not household mix.

**Run this whole pattern twice — once against 2023 (today), once against
2055 (long-range Needs)**, proposed as part of the initial build rather than
a later add-on (see "Decisions needed" above). The diagram below shows one
vintage; the 2055 pass is the identical pattern against the 2055 network and
2055 SE forecast instead.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    SE["Base SE data<br/>(2023 or 2055)"] --> Base["Base run<br/>no HH added"]
    SE -->|"+N HH at Murray"| Control["Control run"]
    SE -->|"+N HH at Site A"| SiteA["Test: Site A"]
    SE -->|"+N HH at Site B"| SiteB["Test: Site B"]
    SE -->|"+N HH at Site ..."| SiteN["Test: Site ..."]

    Base --> Metric["Delta VHT = Test minus Base<br/>peak periods, congested V/C tiers"]
    Control --> Metric
    SiteA --> Metric
    SiteB --> Metric
    SiteN --> Metric

    Metric --> Index["Burden Index(site) =<br/>Delta VHT(site) / Delta VHT(Murray control)"]
```

**Metric:** systemwide congested vehicle-hours-traveled (ΔVHT), not just the
new households' own trips — the whole point is capturing the delay imposed
on *everyone else*, which only shows up as a regionwide before/after
difference. Peak periods (AM, PM), filtered to links at or above a
congestion threshold (V/C ≥ 0.8 and/or ≥ 1.0).

**Burden Index** = ΔVHT(site) ÷ ΔVHT(Murray control) — giving the
"1.6x" / "1.2x" style figure directly, computed separately for 2023 and
2055 so the two years can be compared side by side.

::: {.callout-note}
## A caveat on comparing 2023 and 2055 directly
N households is a much bigger *relative* bump against a TAZ's 2023
household count than against its 2055 forecast, which already assumes
decades of organic growth at these sites. A rising or falling Burden Index
between the two years could partly reflect that shrinking relative size,
not just a real shift in how the network absorbs growth at that location —
worth calling out when the results are reported, not something the study
design itself corrects for.
:::

## Baseline signal, from the registered `base` scenario

These are real numbers from an already-completed model run — not simulated
for illustration. That run is the region's current (2023) road network
exactly as it exists today, with no new households added yet; reusing it
here meant no new traffic-model run was needed just to produce this table.
It shows how congested the road network already is, by time of day, using
the same "how congested" math (V/C ≥ 0.8 and ≥ 1.0 — road segments running
at or above 80%/100% of their capacity) that will measure each candidate
site's impact later.

```{python}
#| label: baseline-table
#| output: asis

runs = rd.latest_run_per_scenario(RUN_SET_ID)
base_run = next(r for r in runs if r["scenario_id"] == "base")
seg_rel_path = next(
    p for p in rd.curated_output_paths(base_run) if p.endswith("_Summary_SEGID_filtered.csv")
)
seg_df = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(rd.REPO_ROOT, seg_rel_path), skipinitialspace=True)

rows = []
for period in ["AM", "MD", "PM", "EV"]:
    vc = pd.to_numeric(seg_df[f"{period}_VC"], errors="coerce")
    vht = pd.to_numeric(seg_df[f"{period}_VHT"], errors="coerce")
    total = vht.sum()
    c08 = vht[vc >= 0.8].sum()
    c10 = vht[vc >= 1.0].sum()
    rows.append(
        f"| {period} | {total:,.0f} | {c08:,.0f} ({c08 / total:.1%}) | {c10:,.0f} ({c10 / total:.1%}) |"
    )

lane_miles = pd.to_numeric(seg_df["LANEMILES"], errors="coerce").sum()

print("| Period | Total VHT | VHT at V/C ≥ 0.8 | VHT at V/C ≥ 1.0 |")
print("|---|---:|---:|---:|")
print("\n".join(rows))
print(f"\nRegionwide lane-miles in this network: **{lane_miles:,.0f}** (segment-direction rows).")
```

This is *system scale*, not the site-comparison metric itself — it's today's
regionwide congested-VHT backdrop that a 500–1000-household ΔVHT would be
measured against. PM is the most congested period by a wide margin; AM is a
distant second; MD and EV carry almost no V/C≥1.0 congestion. This confirms
AM+PM is the right peak-period scope for the Burden Index, and suggests PM
alone may show the clearest site-to-site differences.

::: {.callout-note}
## What's still missing for Control/Test scenarios
This `base` scenario only has the segment summary curated so far — the
regionwide *congestion-tier* summary (`Summary_HighwayNet.csv`, needed for
the Δ calculation once Control/Test scenarios exist) requires the
custom driver-script edit described below, then re-registering `base` with
that output included too. A 2055 counterpart to this `base` scenario
doesn't exist yet either — it needs the same one-step `import-manual-run`
registration against the `v10.0-beta.2` run set's already-run `Needs_2055`
scenario, no new Cube Voyager run required (see "How this fits
the run-management framework" below). Adding Control/Test scenarios for
either year still needs real Cube Voyager runs — see "Decisions needed" and
"Effort and runtime" below.
:::

## Candidate sites

::: {.callout-note}
Candidates, not yet confirmed. Data-driven, but the final pick is a
decision for the study lead — see "Decisions needed" above.

Method: spatially joined the TDM's own TAZ shapefile
(`tdm/1_Inputs/1_TAZ/WFv1000_TAZ.shp`) against WFRC's **Wasatch Choice 2050
Centers (Vision Map)** feature service — the actual regional-centers layer
referenced in the original ask, queried live from
`services1.arcgis.com/taguadKoI1XFwivx/.../Wasatch_Choice_2050_Centers_(Vision_Map)/FeatureServer`
— then cross-referenced household counts from `SE_2023.csv`. Household/city
figures below are pulled live from those same local files on every render.

```{python}
#| label: candidate-sites-map
#| fig-align: center

import json
import math
import geopandas as gpd
import plotly.graph_objects as go

taz_path = os.path.join(rd.REPO_ROOT, "tdm", "1_Inputs", "1_TAZ", "WFv1000_TAZ.shp")
taz_gdf = gpd.read_file(taz_path)
taz_gdf["TAZID"] = taz_gdf["TAZID"].astype(int)

se_path = os.path.join(rd.REPO_ROOT, "tdm", "1_Inputs", "2_SEData", "WFRC", "SE_2023.csv")
se_df = pd.read_csv(se_path)
se_df = se_df.rename(columns={se_df.columns[0]: "TAZID"})
taz_gdf = taz_gdf.merge(se_df[["TAZID", "TOTHH", "HHPOP"]], on="TAZID", how="left")

# category / recommended appended as elements 4/5 -- element indices 0-3
# (label, TAZID, city, note) are unchanged from the table cell below.
# category is just "typical (sprawl)" vs. "center" vs. the Murray control --
# which region a site is in is carried by its label/city instead of a
# separate color, so the map stays readable as more regions get added.
candidates = [
    ("Murray control", 1619, "Murray", "Populous, ordinary residential TAZ -- geographic-center reference", "Murray control", True),
    ("Western Davis -- typical (recommended)", 684, "Syracuse", "Large low-density subdivision, no designated center nearby", "Typical (sprawl)", True),
    ("Western Davis -- typical (alternate)", 602, "West Point", "Further west by X-coordinate; smaller sample", "Typical (sprawl)", False),
    ("Davis CTC -- Syracuse City Center (recommended)", 674, "Syracuse", "Same city as the recommended typical site -- isolates center-vs-not", "City/Town Center", True),
    ("Davis CTC -- Clinton Town Center (alternate)", 610, "Clinton", "", "City/Town Center", False),
    ("Davis CTC -- West Point City Center (alternate)", 600, "West Point", "", "City/Town Center", False),
    ("Davis CTC -- Station Park, Farmington (alternate, Urban Center)", 780, "Farmington", "Larger/more significant center, for a bigger contrast", "City/Town Center", False),
    ("SW Salt Lake County -- typical (recommended)", 2048, "Herriman", "Largest typical TAZ in the county's southwest corner", "Typical (sprawl)", True),
    ("SW Salt Lake County -- typical (alternate)", 2066, "Riverton", "", "Typical (sprawl)", False),
    ("SW Salt Lake CTC -- Herriman Town Center (recommended)", 2039, "Herriman", "Same city as the recommended typical site -- isolates center-vs-not", "City/Town Center", True),
    ("SW Salt Lake CTC -- Downtown Riverton (alternate)", 2080, "Riverton", "", "City/Town Center", False),
    ("Western Utah County -- typical (recommended)", 2467, "Eagle Mountain", "Largest typical TAZ among the newly added target areas", "Typical (sprawl)", True),
    ("Western Utah County -- typical (alternate)", 2519, "Saratoga Springs", "", "Typical (sprawl)", False),
    ("Western Utah CTC -- Eagle Mountain City Center (recommended)", 2313, "Eagle Mountain", "Same city as the recommended typical site -- isolates center-vs-not", "City/Town Center", True),
    ("Western Utah CTC -- Crossroads, Saratoga Springs (alternate)", 2509, "Saratoga Springs", "", "City/Town Center", False),
]
taz_ids = [c[1] for c in candidates]
label_by_id = {c[1]: c[0] for c in candidates}
note_by_id = {c[1]: c[3] for c in candidates}
category_by_id = {c[1]: c[4] for c in candidates}
recommended_by_id = {c[1]: c[5] for c in candidates}

# Categorical hues (not the literal WFRC brand triad -- navy/amber failed
# the colorblind-safety validator's lightness/chroma checks as map marks;
# these three passed all checks including CVD separation).
CATEGORY_COLORS = {
    "Murray control": "#2a78d6",
    "Typical (sprawl)": "#eb6834",
    "City/Town Center": "#1baf7a",
}

map_gdf = taz_gdf[taz_gdf["TAZID"].isin(taz_ids)].copy()
map_gdf["category"] = map_gdf["TAZID"].map(category_by_id)
map_gdf["recommended"] = map_gdf["TAZID"].map(recommended_by_id)
map_gdf["short_label"] = map_gdf["CITY_NAME"] + " (TAZ " + map_gdf["TAZID"].astype(str) + ")"
centroid_ll = map_gdf.geometry.centroid.to_crs(4326)
map_gdf["cx"] = centroid_ll.x
map_gdf["cy"] = centroid_ll.y
map_gdf = map_gdf.to_crs(4326)

fig = go.Figure()
for cat, color in CATEGORY_COLORS.items():
    cat_sub = map_gdf[map_gdf["category"] == cat]
    cat_geojson = json.loads(cat_sub[["TAZID", "geometry"]].to_json())
    rec_suffix = cat_sub["recommended"].map({True: " (recommended)", False: " (alternate)"})
    fig.add_trace(go.Choroplethmap(
        geojson=cat_geojson,
        locations=cat_sub["TAZID"],
        featureidkey="properties.TAZID",
        z=[1] * len(cat_sub),
        colorscale=[[0, color], [1, color]],
        showscale=False,
        marker={"line": {"width": 1.5, "color": "white"}},
        name=cat,
        showlegend=True,
        hovertext=cat_sub["short_label"] + rec_suffix,
        hoverinfo="text",
    ))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scattermap(
        lat=cat_sub["cy"], lon=cat_sub["cx"],
        mode="text",
        text=cat_sub["short_label"],
        textfont={"size": 11, "color": "#1B3A5C"},
        showlegend=False,
        hoverinfo="skip",
    ))

# Fit zoom/center to whatever candidates exist rather than a fixed value --
# the standard "zoom to fit bounds" formula, so the map keeps framing
# correctly as sites get added or removed. Adapted from the well-known
# Google Maps bounds-to-zoom algorithm.
MAP_WIDTH, MAP_HEIGHT = 900, 550


def _lat_rad(lat):
    s = math.sin(lat * math.pi / 180)
    return math.log((1 + s) / (1 - s)) / 2


lat_min, lat_max = map_gdf["cy"].min(), map_gdf["cy"].max()
lon_min, lon_max = map_gdf["cx"].min(), map_gdf["cx"].max()
lat_fraction = (_lat_rad(lat_max) - _lat_rad(lat_min)) / math.pi
lon_fraction = (lon_max - lon_min) / 360
fit_zoom = min(
    math.log2(MAP_HEIGHT / 256 / max(lat_fraction, 1e-9)),
    math.log2(MAP_WIDTH / 256 / max(lon_fraction, 1e-9)),
) - math.log2(1.15)  # 15% padding so edge markers/labels aren't clipped

fig.update_layout(
    map={
        "style": "carto-positron",
        "zoom": fit_zoom,
        "center": {"lat": (lat_min + lat_max) / 2, "lon": (lon_min + lon_max) / 2},
    },
    height=MAP_HEIGHT,
    margin={"l": 0, "r": 0, "t": 10, "b": 0},
    legend={"orientation": "h", "yanchor": "bottom", "y": 1.0, "xanchor": "left", "x": 0},
)
fig.show(config={"displayModeBar": False})
```

**Recommendation:** start with the Syracuse typical site (684) paired against
the Syracuse City Center (674) — same city, so the comparison isolates
"designated center vs. not" rather than mixing in city-level differences,
which is exactly the contrast the original ask describes. Combined with the
Murray control (1619), that's the minimal 3-scenario build (plus `base`)
needed to prove the methodology end-to-end.

Once that's proven, the recommended **fuller site list** repeats the same
same-city typical-vs-center pairing in two more fast-growing, peripheral
parts of the region (household counts in the table above): Herriman (2048)
vs. Herriman Town Center (2039) for southwest Salt Lake County, and Eagle
Mountain (2467) vs. Eagle Mountain City Center (2313) for western Utah
County. That's 3 typical-vs-center pairs plus Murray — 7 sites total, each
run against both network vintages.

## What the model already gives us to work with

This isn't hypothetical — the pieces exist in the TDM today, just not wired
together for this purpose:

| Need | Existing TDM piece | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Systemwide VMT/VHT by period, purpose, and congestion tier (V/C ≥ 0.8, ≥ 1.0) | `2_ModelScripts/7_PostProcessing/4_BCA_Summaries/02_Summarize_HighwayNet.s` | Exists, does exactly this — but its `READ FILE` line is **commented out** in the default driver script, so it doesn't currently run |
| A way to add households to a specific TAZ without touching anything else | `WFRC_SEFile` / `MAG_SEFile` — plain TAZ-level `TOTHH`/`HHPOP` CSVs | Exists; this framework already has a proven pattern for generating per-scenario SE variants (used for the `non-motorized-2023` study) |
| 2023 and 2055 base networks to build on | The `v10.0-beta.2` run set's `Base_2023` and `Needs_2055` scenarios, both already run in this repo | 2023 **done** — registered as this run set's own `base` scenario via `import-manual-run`. 2055 not yet registered, but the same one-step `import-manual-run` against the already-run `Needs_2055` scenario is all it needs |
| Household composition (size, income, workers, autos) for the "typical household" | `1_HHDisag_AutoOwn/` (LifeCycle → HHDisaggregation → AutoOwnership) | The model derives this itself from `TOTHH`/`HHPOP`, using distributions that already respond to local accessibility — there's no separate lever to force a specific household profile |

## How this fits the run-management framework

Mechanically, this is a new run set — `household-location-burden` —
following the same pattern already proven by `non-motorized-2023` and
`bring-work-trips-closer-to-home`:

- **`base`** (2023) — **done**. Registered by reusing the existing
  `v10.0-beta.2-2023` run rather than re-running full feedback from scratch.
  To pick up the BCA congestion-tier summary once the driver script is
  edited, its raw folder can be re-entered via `start_at_label` (resuming
  just the post-processing steps) rather than a full re-run.
- **`base-2055`** — same treatment, reusing `v10.0-beta.2`'s already-run
  `Needs_2055` scenario. Not yet registered.
- **`control-murray-2023`** / **`control-murray-2055`** and one
  **`site-<name>-2023`** / **`site-<name>-2055`** pair per candidate
  location — each pointed at its own generated SE file (drawn from the
  matching year's SE forecast) via `overrides.WFRC_SEFile`, the same
  relative-path mechanism `non-motorized-2023` uses.
- A shared **custom driver script** (this run set's own copy of
  `__HailMary_1Subfolder.s`, with the BCA summary line turned on) — the
  framework's existing `driver_script` mechanism, no core code changes
  needed.
- **Outputs curated**: just the small `Summary_HighwayNet.csv` per
  scenario — well under the size ceiling, no raw network/matrix files
  committed.
- A small Burden Index calculation module, reported here once real runs
  exist — same shape as `non-motorized-2023`'s `report_loader.py`.

No changes to the TDM codebase, the orchestrator's core logic, or how Cube
Voyager runs are required — this is entirely new configuration plus one
custom driver script, the same category of work as every other run set in
this repo.

## Effort and runtime

Each Test/Control scenario needs a **full feedback run** (mode choice
logsums + four-period assignment) — households are added before
disaggregation, so nothing upstream can be skipped or reused between sites.
Only the two Base runs benefit from reuse (both already run, neither needs
re-running). Running both the 2023 and 2055 vintages roughly doubles
the Test/Control run count for the same site list. For the recommended
7-site list (Murray control + 3 typical-vs-center pairs), that's 1 control
run + 6 test runs, × 2 years = **14 Test/Control runs** against two free
Base runs — before counting any alternates. Runtime scales linearly with
number of sites *and* years; `max_parallel_runs` (already supported, not yet
exercised on a real multi-scenario batch) could help once Cube Voyager
licensing/hardware limits on this workstation are confirmed.

**Why not combine multiple sites into one run?** Congestion is non-linear —
that's the whole reason V/C-tiered VHT is the metric. Adding households from
two sites in the same run gives you their *combined* effect on network
delay, with no way to split credit between them afterward (their trips might
stack on the same congested links, or might not interact at all). Base and
Control aren't combinable either — they're mutually exclusive states of the
same synthetic population. Recovering true per-site effects from combined
runs would need a full factorial design (every combination, solved for
interaction terms), which needs *more* runs than one-at-a-time, not fewer.
So N candidate sites need N separate Test runs against one shared Base — this
design is already the minimal N+1, and the +1 is free (Base is reused, not
re-run).

Suggested build order:
1. Confirm the Base-run reuse strategy and the driver-script edit; validate
   `Summary_HighwayNet.csv` comes out as expected on the existing 2023 Base
   run alone.
2. Register `base-2055` the same way, and confirm it too.
3. Build SE generation + one real site + the Murray control for **2023
   only**; validate the ΔVHT / Burden Index math end-to-end on real output
   before committing to the full site list or the second year.
4. Once proven, replicate that same site + control for **2055**, to confirm
   the pattern holds across both vintages.
5. Add the remaining sites from the confirmed list, for both years.

## Bottom line

The metric, the SE-modification mechanism, and the run-set framework are all
already proven in this repo for other studies — this is a matter of
configuration and one small driver-script change, not new engineering. Every
remaining decision above (N, congestion threshold, peak window, final site
picks, network vintages) has a sensible default, so the build can proceed on
the recommended picks — 2023 and 2055, both — unless told otherwise.
